title: Copy fundamentals (universal rubric for any marketing copy)

gates.text: Truth: no claim, number, customer, quote, story, offer term, deadline or result that isn't in confirmed facts or cited research. Gaps are written around (pick an angle the confirmed facts fully support); never an invention, never a placeholder in publishable copy. VoC phrases are not presented as attributed testimonials without confirmed permission.

Banned language: no phrase from the hard-fail banned list (unless it appears in the owner's own brand-voice samples), no unsourced superlatives (best, #1, leading, fastest), no ALL CAPS words, at most one exclamation mark.
Limits and format: the piece respects the channel's character, hashtag and emoji limits and has exactly one primary CTA.
Policy: no engagement bait (comment YES, tag a friend, like if), no fake urgency or scarcity, no personal-attribute phrasing aimed at the reader.

Voice and promise: on the brand's own channels the copy speaks as the brand (we/our/you), never about it in the third person; every count or promise in a title, hook or alt text is delivered by the piece.

anchors.1: Generic; every key sentence passes the competitor swap test (could be any business).
anchors.3: Some numbers, names or scenes, but the central claim is still vague or could be a competitor's.
anchors.5: Every claim concrete (number, name, time, place, process); the piece is unmistakably this business and fails the swap test everywhere.

anchors.1: No identifiable reader; written in the business's internal or category jargon.
anchors.3: Right segment but a generic situation; customer language absent or paraphrased into marketing-speak.
anchors.5: Speaks to one reader in one moment (the trigger from the positioning), using verbatim or near-verbatim customer phrases for the problem or outcome.

anchors.1: Several competing messages, or a list of features with no through-line.
anchors.3: One main idea with digressions or a second pitch tacked on.
anchors.5: One idea statable in under 12 words, fully developed; every line serves it and each paragraph follows from the last.

anchors.1: Claims with no support, or support that is a superlative.
anchors.3: Some proof present but not next to the claims it supports, or weakest proof used when stronger was available.
anchors.5: Each claim has evidence within two sentences; the strongest available proof (number, named quote, mechanism) appears in the first third.

anchors.1: Says that it works, never how.
anchors.3: Mechanism mentioned but abstract ("our proven process").
anchors.5: Explains the concrete how (step, ingredient, rule, tool) in plain words, so the reader believes the outcome.

anchors.1: Throat-clearing, brand intro or a generic truth.
anchors.3: Clear topic but predictable; no tension or specific detail.
anchors.5: Stops the reader with a specific number, scene or tension in the first line, and the body pays it off completely.

anchors.1: Robotic: AI tells, framework seams, uniform sentence lengths, disconnected slogans.
anchors.3: Clean but bland; could be any brand's house style.
anchors.5: Sounds like this owner or brand (matches voice samples); varied sentence length; reads naturally aloud at the right reading level.

anchors.1: Missing, vague ("Learn more") or several competing asks.
anchors.3: One clear ask, but generic or higher-friction than the awareness level allows.
anchors.5: One specific, low-friction action matched to awareness level, with the outcome stated and only true friction-removers.

anchors.1: Contradicts or ignores the positioning (wrong customer, wrong alternative, off-brand claim).
anchors.3: Consistent with the positioning but doesn't express a specific pillar, objection or alternative.
anchors.5: Clearly expresses one positioning element (value pillar, objection counter, alternative's trade-off or trigger moment) in reader language, without pasting positioning jargon.
